section.title: The Shoot from Jesse
section.sectionRationale: Immediately after the felled forest of Assyria's pride, a very different tree image appears: a tender shoot rising from the stump of Jesse, David's father, empowered by the Spirit to rule with perfect justice and to inaugurate a peace so complete that predator and prey lie down together. The chapter closes with the regathering of a scattered remnant, tying this messianic vision back to Israel's own restoration.
section.thesis: From the humbled line of David, apparently as dead as a felled tree, the Spirit-anointed shoot will rise to judge with perfect righteousness, secure a peace that undoes creation's violence, and become a banner drawing the nations and gathering God's scattered people home.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the Spirit-filled shoot from Jesse's stump and His righteous judgment; the peaceable kingdom where creation's violence is undone; the root of Jesse as a banner to the nations; and the second exodus gathering the remnant home.

units.label: The Spirit-filled shoot
units.note: wisdom, might, and the fear of the LORD

verses.text: Then a {{choter|shoot}} will spring up from the stump of Jesse, and a {{netzer|Branch}} from his roots will bear fruit.

The {{ruach2|Spirit}} of the LORD will rest on Him, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, 
the Spirit of counsel and strength, 
the Spirit of knowledge and fear of the LORD.

And He will delight in the fear of the LORD. 
He will not judge by what His eyes see, and He will not decide by what His ears hear,

but with righteousness He will judge the poor, and with equity He will decide for the lowly of the earth. He will strike the earth with the rod of His mouth and slay the wicked with the breath of His lips.
Righteousness will be the belt around His hips, and faithfulness the sash around His waist.

units.label: The peaceable kingdom
units.note: the wolf and the lamb together

verses.text: The wolf will live with the lamb, and the leopard will lie down with the goat; the calf and young lion and fatling will be together, and a little child will lead them.

The cow will graze with the bear, their young will lie down together, 
and the lion will eat straw like the ox.
The infant will play by the cobra's den, and the toddler will reach into the viper's nest.
They will neither harm nor destroy on all My holy mountain, for the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the sea is full of water.

units.label: A banner to the nations
units.note: the Root of Jesse sought by the peoples

verses.text: On that day the Root of Jesse will stand as a banner for the peoples. The nations will seek Him, and His place of rest will be glorious.

On that day the Lord will extend His hand a second time to recover the remnant of His people from Assyria, from Egypt, from Pathros, from Cush, from Elam, from Shinar, from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea.
He will raise a banner for the nations and gather the exiles of Israel; He will collect the scattered of Judah from the four corners of the earth.
Then the jealousy of Ephraim will depart, and the adversaries of Judah will be cut off. Ephraim will no longer envy Judah, nor will Judah harass Ephraim.

They will swoop down on the slopes of the Philistines to the west; together they will plunder the sons of the east. They will lay their hands on Edom and Moab, and the Ammonites will be subject to them.

The LORD will devote to destruction the gulf of the Sea of Egypt; with a scorching wind He will sweep His hand over the Euphrates. He will split it into seven streams for men to cross with dry sandals.
There will be a highway for the remnant of His people who remain from Assyria, as there was for Israel when they came up from the land of Egypt.

choter.gloss: A shoot, twig, or young sprout, a fragile-sounding word for new growth springing from what looked like a dead stump. The image deliberately follows the felled forest of Assyria's pride in chapter 10, contrasting worldly imperial power with the humble, Spirit-empowered rise of David's promised heir.

netzer.gloss: Branch, sprout, a term closely related to the tsemach of Isaiah 4:2 and likely the wordplay behind Matthew's reference to Jesus as a Nazarene, Matthew 2:23, since Nazareth's name may derive from this same root, a small town aptly named for the humble Branch who grew up there.

ruach2.gloss: Spirit, wind, breath. The sevenfold description here, the Spirit of the LORD, wisdom, understanding, counsel, strength, knowledge, and the fear of the LORD, forms the traditional 'sevenfold Spirit' pattern later echoed in Revelation 5:6's seven Spirits of God before the Lamb's throne.

basic.context: Immediately after Assyria's proud forest is felled at the end of chapter 10, a very different image appears: a small shoot springing from the stump of Jesse, David's father, a picture of new life from what looked like a finished, dead line. This shoot is filled with the Spirit of the LORD, judges the poor with perfect righteousness, and inaugurates such complete peace that natural predators lie down with their former prey. The chapter closes with this same figure, now called the Root of Jesse, drawing the nations to Himself and gathering God's scattered people home in a second exodus.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a genuine messianic prophecy describing a coming individual ruler from David's line, whose Spirit-empowered wisdom, perfect justice, and peace-bringing reign go beyond what any historical Davidic king, including Hezekiah, ever achieved. The honest tension in the chapter is how the vivid peaceable-kingdom imagery, wolves with lambs, relates to the more clearly future-oriented promises of gathering exiles; the pattern of near expectation and ultimate fulfillment found throughout Isaiah suggests both a genuinely inaugurated present reality in Christ and a still-awaited fullness in the new creation.
basic.originalLanguages: A choter, tender shoot, rises from the stump of Jesse, and a netzer, branch, from his roots bears fruit, imagery so central it may lie behind Matthew's description of Jesus as a Nazarene. The sevenfold ruach, Spirit, of the LORD, wisdom, understanding, counsel, strength, knowledge, and the fear of the LORD, rests on this figure, forming a pattern later echoed in Revelation's seven Spirits before the Lamb's throne.
basic.typology: The shoot from Jesse's stump directly fulfills the promise of the Branch first introduced in Isaiah 4:2, and its rise from apparent devastation typifies resurrection life emerging from death itself. The peaceable kingdom where the wolf lies down with the lamb anticipates the full undoing of creation's fall under Christ's final reign, and the second exodus gathering exiles from every direction previews the ingathering of God's people from every nation into Christ.
basic.christ: Paul quotes Isaiah 11:10 directly in Romans 15:12, applying the Root of Jesse's role as a banner drawing the nations explicitly to Christ's mission to the Gentiles, and Jesus applies Isaiah's language of the Spirit resting on Him to Himself in Luke 4:18, quoting the closely related Isaiah 61:1. Revelation 5:5 identifies Jesus as the Root of David, directly picking up this chapter's title, the conquering Lion who is also the slain Lamb, worthy to open the scroll of history.
basic.god: God brings new, Spirit-empowered life out of what appears to be a completely dead situation, David's line reduced to a bare stump, showing His redemptive pattern of resurrection out of apparent finality. His justice for the poor and lowly, exercised not by mere appearance but by true discernment, reveals a character committed to genuine righteousness rather than superficial judgment, a character He now shares fully with His anointed King.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 4:2 first introduces the Branch of the LORD, developed further here as the shoot from Jesse's stump. Luke 4:18 has Jesus apply Spirit-anointed, justice-bringing language to Himself directly. Romans 15:12 quotes Isaiah 11:10 explicitly regarding Christ's mission to draw the Gentiles. Revelation 5:5 names Jesus the Root of David, the Lion of the tribe of Judah who is also the slain Lamb.
basic.oneStory: This chapter shows God's pattern of bringing overwhelming new life out of apparent devastation: a tender shoot from a felled and stumped line becomes the Spirit-filled King who judges rightly, secures true peace, and draws the nations to Himself. That shoot is Jesus, the Root and offspring of David, in whom the whole story of Israel's scattering and gathering finds its true, climactic fulfillment.

context.literary:
Isaiah 11 is the second half of a pair with 10:33-34, and the pair is a single stroke of the pen. Chapter 10 ends with the axe at work in the forest: 'He will clear the forest thickets with an axe, and Lebanon will fall.' Chapter 11 begins in the same stand of timber, only now at ground level, with a cut stump and a green shoot. The English chapter division makes a break where Isaiah made a join. The two images do not merely contrast; one produces the other. The felling clears the ground, and out of what looks like the end, a beginning comes.

Within the chapter there are two halves, and each has its own geography. Verses 1 to 9 stay in one place, the 'holy mountain,' and look at what happens there when the King reigns. Verses 10 to 16 look outward to the nations and the scattered exiles and describe a great gathering. The phrase 'on that day' opens verses 10 and 11 and marks the hinge. The first half is about the King's person and the peace He brings; the second is about the movement of peoples toward Him.

The first half has its own order. Verses 1 to 2 name the shoot and His equipment, the Spirit. Verses 3 to 5 describe how He judges and what He wears: the way He decides, the poor and lowly He defends, the wicked He strikes, and the belt of righteousness and faithfulness. Verses 6 to 9 show the result in nature, and verse 9 gives the reason: the knowledge of the LORD. Each step grows from the one before. A King who judges truly makes a peace that reaches the animals, and this is because the earth fills with the knowledge of God.

The verses on the peaceable kingdom are written as a catalogue of pairs. Predator and prey are named, then the domestic and the wild, then the child and the serpent. The pairs are arranged so that the movement goes from the strongest animals to the weakest human, the child and the infant, at the nest of the cobra. The poet takes the most dangerous thing and puts the most vulnerable person beside it.

The second half gathers its energy from one repeated verb of raising: the root stands as a banner, verse 10, and the LORD raises a banner, verse 12. The picture of a lifted signal over the nations is at the centre of the gathering.
context.historical:
When Isaiah first spoke this, the house of David was under siege in a double sense. Aram and Ephraim had marched on Jerusalem in the days of Ahaz, so that the hearts of the king and his people 'trembled like trees in the forest shaken by the wind,' Isaiah 7:2. Then came the greater threat of Assyria, and Isaiah has just said, in chapter 10, that the forest of that empire will be cut down. The stump of Jesse, therefore, is first of all a real possibility: the Davidic house, reduced to its roots, could be cut off.

The name Jesse is a striking choice. Isaiah does not say 'the stump of David' or 'of Solomon.' The royal house is traced to its beginning in the unremarkable family of Jesse of Bethlehem, a man whose son was selected by God when the reigning king had been rejected, 1 Samuel 16:1. The humble origin may be part of the point. God can begin again where He began before, with a shepherd family from a small town. Centuries later Micah says that the ruler will come from Bethlehem, 'small among the clans of Judah,' Micah 5:2.

The second half of the chapter reflects the actual situation of the people of God after the Assyrian conquests. The Assyrian policy of deportation had already scattered the northern tribes, and the places named in verse 11 map the dispersion: Assyria and Egypt, Pathros in upper Egypt, Cush to the south, Elam and Shinar to the east, Hamath to the north, and the 'islands of the sea' to the west. Many of these came to hold Jewish communities in later centuries, which is how the promise was heard by exiles of every era.

The chapter would have been read by the exiles after 586 BC as a promise for the return from Babylon, and the return under Cyrus in 538 BC did bring a first regathering. Yet the later prophets, and the New Testament, continued to say that the shoot had not yet fully come. The Davidic throne was empty during and after the return. The oracle therefore lived in Israel as a promise held in trust, awaiting the King, and is cited in the Jewish literature of the Second Temple period as an expectation of the Messiah.
context.canonical:
The shoot has a family of its own in Scripture. Isaiah 4:2 had already said, 'the Branch of the LORD will be beautiful and glorious.' Jeremiah takes up the figure: 'I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, and He will reign wisely as King and will administer justice and righteousness in the land,' Jeremiah 23:5. Ezekiel speaks of one shepherd, 'My servant David,' who will make a covenant of peace and 'rid the land of wild animals,' Ezekiel 34:23-25. Zechariah names the Branch as a man, a priest on his throne. The royal hope grows through these voices, and every one of them goes back to the Davidic covenant of 2 Samuel 7.

Within Isaiah the chapter takes its place beside the other pictures of the coming ruler. The child of 9:6-7 bears the government. The Servant of Isaiah 42:1 has the Spirit put on Him and brings justice to the nations, and the anointed one of Isaiah 61:1 has the Spirit on Him to bring good news to the poor. Isaiah 53:2 says of the Servant that 'He grew up before Him like a tender shoot, and like a root out of dry ground.' The description of Isaiah 11 is the royal face of a figure whose suffering face is shown later. The peaceable mountain returns at the end of the book, in Isaiah 65:25, and Isaiah 2:2-4 describes the same mountain as the place to which the nations stream and from which law goes out.

In the New Testament the chapter is a main source for Jesus' identity. Paul quotes verse 10 to show that Christ's mission to the Gentiles was foretold: 'The Root of Jesse will appear, One who will arise to rule over the Gentiles; in Him the Gentiles will put their hope,' Romans 15:12. John the Baptist sees the Spirit 'descending from heaven like a dove and resting on Him,' John 1:32. Matthew places Jesse in the genealogy, Matthew 1:5-6, and the elder in Revelation 5:5 says that 'the Root of David, has triumphed.' Jesus Himself, in the last chapter of the Bible, says, 'I am the Root and the Offspring of David,' Revelation 22:16. The oracle stands at the beginning and the end of the Bible's account of the King.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Isaiah meant to give the people of Judah a reason to hope when the visible house of David looked finished. They had just heard that the Assyrian forest would be cut down, and a listener might ask what then would happen to the king's family, which was also a tree under threat. Isaiah's answer is that God does not need the grand structure. A stump is enough, because the life is in the root and the root is God's promise.

He also meant to teach what a true king is. Kings in Judah had often been judged by how they looked and what they heard, and Isaiah describes a King who does neither. He will 'not judge by what His eyes see' or 'decide by what His ears hear.' The test of a king is what he does for the poor. This gave the hearers a standard by which to measure the kings they actually had, and to see how far they had come from Ahaz's way of governing by alliance and fear.

He wanted them to hope for a peace that goes all the way down. The wolf and the lamb are not a mere decoration but a statement that when this King reigns, the creation's violence ends, and the reason given is a knowledge of the LORD that floods the earth. Violence is not only a matter of politics; it is a matter of knowing God.

Finally the gathering of the exiles and the end of the quarrel between Ephraim and Judah told them that the break that Assyria had caused was not final. God would call His scattered people, north and south, and heal the old division. The hearers were meant to see that the LORD would do for them what He did in Egypt, and more.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage is promise, and most of it is in the future tense: 'will spring up,' 'will rest,' 'will judge,' 'will live.' It does not command believers to produce the peaceable kingdom, and it would be a mistake to read the lion eating straw as a programme for politics or ecology. What believers are given is a hope and a picture of what the King will do.

What the passage does prescribe by implication is the shape of righteous judgment. The King's judging of the poor with righteousness and the lowly with equity is a standard for every human exercise of authority, whether by a magistrate, an employer, a church elder or a parent. Believers are not the shoot, but they are asked to imitate His justice where they have authority: to look past appearance and rumour, and to give a hearing to the person without a voice. Jesus echoes this when He tells His hearers, 'Stop judging by outward appearances, and start judging justly,' John 7:24.

The passage also shapes how to read prophecy. The details of verses 14 to 16, the plundering of Philistia and the conquest of Edom and Moab, belong to the idiom of Israel's world, and the New Testament does not take them as a call for war. They speak of the victory of God's King over the nations that opposed His people. The church's calling, set out in places such as Ephesians 6:14, is a spiritual fight carried out with truth and righteousness, the very things the King wears in verse 5, and not with the sword.

debates.question: Is the peaceable kingdom of verses 6-9 describing a future, still-unrealized new creation, a present spiritual reality already inaugurated in Christ, or both?

views.label: A future, literal new creation
views.case: The complete absence of predatory violence, wolf with lamb and lion eating straw, has not happened in the physical world, so many read this as awaiting the new heavens and new earth. Isaiah 65:25 repeats the picture and puts it in 'new heavens and a new earth,' and Paul says that creation itself 'will be set free from its slavery to corruption,' Romans 8:21.

views.label: A symbol of reconciled people in Christ now
views.case: The reason given in verse 9 is that 'the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD,' and that is already advancing through the gospel. On this view the animals picture enemies made into one body, such as Jew and Gentile in Ephesians 2:14-16, and the peace is realized in the church as a first fruit.

debates.bearing: The two readings are not rivals if Isaiah's pattern of near and far is held. The peace begins wherever the King is known and is complete only when He has put all things right. The restored harmony of Mark 1:13, where Jesus is 'with the wild animals' in the wilderness, hints at how deep the restoration goes.

debates.question: Does the second gathering of verses 11 to 16 refer to the return from Babylon, to the gathering of people into Christ and His church, or to a still future gathering of ethnic Israel?

views.label: The return from exile, with later echoes
views.case: The oracle speaks of a gathering from Assyria and Egypt and the rest, and the return from Babylon under Cyrus began such a gathering. Yet the return was small, and the places named go well beyond Babylon, so this reading regards the oracle as only partly fulfilled in the return.

views.label: The gathering of God's people in Christ
views.case: Jesus died 'not only for the nation, but also for the scattered children of God, to gather them together into one,' John 11:52. Paul reads the Gentiles' hope in the Root of Jesse, Romans 15:12, and the healing of Ephraim and Judah finds its sense in the one new man of Ephesians 2:15. On this view the banner is the cross, and the gathering takes place in the church from every nation.

views.label: A still future restoration of national Israel
views.case: Others point to the specific geography and to the promise of a second gathering from the four corners of the earth, and hold that Paul's hope for 'all Israel' in Romans 11:26 means a further restoration in the land and in faith before or at the return of Christ.

debates.bearing: Christians have read these verses in each of these ways, and the three do not have to exclude one another. All agree that the shoot is the focus of the gathering and that God's promise to scattered people will not fail.

debates.question: Who is the shoot: a king of Isaiah's own day, a later son of David, or the final Messiah?

views.label: A near Davidic king such as Hezekiah
views.case: Isaiah's first hearers lived under Hezekiah, who was a reforming king in David's line, and some Jewish and critical interpreters read the oracle as an idealized picture of such a ruler, or of a king after the exile.

views.label: The ideal and final Messiah
views.case: The Spirit's sevenfold equipment, the peace that reaches to the animals and the world-wide knowledge of the LORD go beyond any king of Judah. The Jewish tradition of the Second Temple period read the passage of the Messiah, and the New Testament does the same, as in Romans 15:12 and Revelation 5:5.

debates.bearing: A particular king may have been in Isaiah's eye as the first sign of the pattern, but no king in David's line fulfilled the full picture. The long wait for a King who would is part of the force of the promise.

study.originalLanguages:
The first image has two Hebrew words that the basic study names, but the words around them add to the picture. The stump is geza, the cut-off trunk of a felled tree. Job 14:7-9 uses the same word family for the hope of a tree: 'If it is cut down, it will sprout again... its stump dies in the soil, at the scent of water it will bud.' Isaiah borrows this ordinary fact of life and applies it to a dynasty. And the shoot grows 'from his roots,' shoresh, a word that returns in verse 10 for the 'Root of Jesse.' The shoot of verse 1 and the root of verse 10 are the same figure from below and above: He is what springs from the root and the root itself. The Septuagint of verse 10 says 'the root of Jesse' and has him 'arising to rule the Gentiles,' where the Hebrew speaks of standing as a banner, and Paul quotes this Greek form in Romans 15:12.

The Spirit's equipment in verse 2 is organized in pairs. Wisdom and understanding, counsel and strength, knowledge and fear of the LORD. The pairs move from the mind, to the practical, to the relationship with God. The Hebrew lists six qualities and then repeats the fear of the LORD in verse 3, which is how later readers reached seven; the Septuagint renders the first 'fear' with a word for godliness, which makes the tradition of seven clearer. Revelation's seven Spirits before the throne, Revelation 5:6, builds on this. The verb 'rest' in 'will rest on Him' comes from nuach, the root behind menuchah, 'resting place,' in verse 10. The Spirit rests on the King, and His own resting place is glorious, so that He is both a bearer and a giver of rest. John says that the Spirit descended and 'remained' on Jesus, John 1:32-33.

In verse 3 the phrase 'He will delight in the fear of the LORD' uses a verb built on the root for scent or breath, and the sense is that the fear of the LORD is the air He breathes. The King enjoys what others dread. Joined to the next phrases about not judging by eyes and ears, the verse says that He is governed by the fear of God rather than by appearance and rumour.

Verse 4 describes the King's justice with the word mishor, 'equity,' whose root idea is level ground, the opposite of the rough and uneven ground that Isaiah 40:4 says will be made a plain. Equity is the levelling of the field for those the powerful have tilted against. The 'rod of His mouth' is again shevet, the word that Isaiah 10:5 used for Assyria, but now the weapon is speech: the King slays by breath. Paul uses the same picture for the Lord Jesus who will 'slay with the breath of His mouth,' 2 Thessalonians 2:8.

In verse 6 the wolf 'will live with' the lamb, using a verb, gur, that means to dwell as a guest or sojourner. The wolf becomes a guest in the lamb's house, which is a picture of hospitality in place of hunting.

Verse 10 says the Root 'will stand as a banner,' nes. The same word is used for the pole on which Moses lifted the bronze serpent in the wilderness, Numbers 21:8-9, and the rescue came by looking. The banner is something lifted and seen. The nations 'will seek' Him, a verb of inquiry that is used for seeking God in worship.

In verse 11 the LORD 'will extend His hand a second time to recover' the remnant. The verb 'recover' is the one for acquiring or buying, and it recalls the exodus song, 'the people You have bought,' Exodus 15:16. The second exodus is a second purchase. And the verb in verse 15, 'devote to destruction,' is the word used for the ban on the cities of Canaan; it is turned here on the sea itself, so that the barrier is removed as a thing set apart for God.

typology.fulfillment: A felled line puts out a green shoot, and Job 14:7-9 shows the hope of a tree cut down. In Isaiah 53:2 the Servant grows 'like a root out of dry ground,' and in Christ the picture finds its fulfilment in a more literal sense: a Son born of David's line in a time when the dynasty seemed dead, Matthew 1:5-6 and Luke 3:23-38. His resurrection is life out of what was cut off, Acts 2:30-32. The type falls short in that the shoot of Isaiah 11 is a new branch from the old tree, while the risen Christ is the root and the life of the tree itself, Revelation 22:16.

typology.type: The Spirit resting on the ruler, Isaiah 11:2
typology.fulfillment: The Spirit of the LORD came on judges and kings, on Gideon, Samson and David, 1 Samuel 16:13, for a time and for a task. In Isaiah the Spirit rests, which suggests permanence. At Jesus' baptism the Spirit descends and remains, John 1:32-33, and God 'gives the Spirit without limit,' John 3:34. The earlier bearers were given the Spirit for a task; the Son has the Spirit as His own, and the Spirit goes out from Him to His people, Acts 2:33.

The picture takes the hearer back to Eden, where creatures were given plants to eat, Genesis 1:30, and forward to the new creation, where creation is 'set free from its slavery to corruption,' Romans 8:21. In Jesus' temptation He is 'with the wild animals, and the angels ministered to Him,' Mark 1:13, a hint of Eden restored in the person of the second Adam, though Mark does not draw the connection. The type is not fulfilled yet in its physical scope, since the creation still groans, and it falls short in the first Eden in that its peace could be broken. Isaiah says the new peace will be secured by the knowledge of the LORD, which cannot be lost.

typology.type: The banner lifted for the nations, Isaiah 11:10
typology.fulfillment: The same word, nes, is used for the pole carrying the bronze serpent, Numbers 21:8-9. Jesus says, 'Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up,' John 3:14-15, and 'I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to Myself,' John 12:32. The correspondence is that a lifted object saves those who look to it. The escalation is that the pole of the wilderness healed Israel for a season, and the cross draws the nations and gives eternal life.

typology.type: The second exodus and the highway, Isaiah 11:15-16
typology.fulfillment: The Lord splits the Euphrates into seven streams for men to cross 'with dry sandals,' and builds a highway for the remnant 'as there was for Israel when they came up from the land of Egypt.' Isaiah 40:3 picks up the highway, and the Gospels apply it to John's work of preparing the way for Jesus, Mark 1:2-3. On the mount of transfiguration Moses and Elijah speak with Jesus about His 'departure,' the Greek word being exodus, 'which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem,' Luke 9:31. The pattern is fulfilled in His journey through death to a new life for His people, and it falls short in the first exodus because that one led to Canaan and this one to a new creation.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ first by the family line. Matthew's genealogy places Jesse in the middle: 'Obed the father of Jesse, and Jesse the father of David the king,' Matthew 1:5-6. The long list of names, with its dark episodes and its exile, is the stump. And in the middle of that list a child is born in Bethlehem, the town of Jesse, as Micah foretold, Micah 5:2. Jesus comes from the root in the very place Isaiah's words suggest, a small town and a humble family when the dynasty has no throne. Isaiah 53:2, 'a tender shoot... a root out of dry ground,' is the same picture from the Servant's side.

It leads to Christ by the Spirit. The Spirit's sevenfold rest on the shoot is what the Gospels show at the Jordan: the Spirit descended and remained, John 1:32-33, and the voice from heaven declared, 'You are My beloved Son,' Luke 3:22. Peter summarizes: 'God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power,' Acts 10:38. Even in the child the Gospels notice what Isaiah promised: 'He was filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was upon Him,' Luke 2:40. Jesus, when He reads Isaiah 61, adds, 'The Spirit of the Lord is on Me,' Luke 4:18, and says that it was fulfilled that day.

It leads to Christ by the way He judges. Isaiah says He will not judge by eyes and ears, and John says of Jesus that He 'did not need any testimony about man, for He knew what was in a man,' John 2:25. He judges the poor with righteousness, and He is the one before whom the lowly, the leper and the woman at the well, are seen as they are. He could say to His critics, 'Stop judging by outward appearances, and start judging justly,' John 7:24, because He did so Himself. The rod of His mouth is the word that will end evil: the Lord Jesus will 'slay with the breath of His mouth,' 2 Thessalonians 2:8, and from His mouth 'proceeds a sharp sword,' Revelation 19:15.

It leads to Christ by the banner and the nations. Paul quotes verse 10 and says that this shoot would 'arise to rule over the Gentiles,' Romans 15:12, and that the Gentiles would hope in Him. Jesus said that when He was lifted up He would draw all people to Himself, John 12:32, and the vision of Revelation is of 'a multitude too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue,' Revelation 7:9. Ephesians shows the healing of the old quarrel between those near and far, as He 'made the two one' and created 'in Himself one new man out of the two,' Ephesians 2:14-15. Ephraim and Judah, those who had harassed each other, are replaced by Jew and Gentile at peace.

It leads to Christ by the Lion and the Lamb. In Revelation the elder tells John that 'the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has triumphed,' and when John looks he sees 'a Lamb who appeared to have been slain,' Revelation 5:5-6, with seven eyes that are the seven Spirits of God. Isaiah's shoot is the Root and the King who conquers; John sees that He conquers as the Lamb. In the last chapter Jesus says, 'I am the Root and the Offspring of David,' Revelation 22:16, the one who both comes from the line and is its source.

A caution is needed. Not every picture in the chapter is a code for an event in Jesus' life: the wolf and the lamb are not a puzzle to be matched to Gospel scenes. The New Testament uses verse 1 to 5 and verse 10 and shows that the person is Christ; the rest of the chapter describes what He will bring. Matthew's Nazarene is not a quotation of this chapter but an allusion at most. The picture is whole when the reader sees the King and then waits for the kingdom.
study.god:
The first thing the chapter shows about God is that He makes new life from what looks finished. Isaiah has just described the felling of every proud thing, and then he says that a shoot springs up. This is not a repair of the old tree but a new thing from the old root. The shoot comes because God has bound Himself to David, and the stump is the guarantee that His promise did not depend on how healthy the tree looked. It is the same pattern as Sarah's womb and the empty tomb: where human possibility ends, God begins.

He is the giver of the Spirit and the source of all wisdom and strength. The six names of the Spirit in verse 2 describe the resources of God, given to a human King. Wisdom, counsel, might and knowledge are what the nations tried to find in their kings and what God Himself supplies. The King's authority is therefore never merely His own, and everything He does is the LORD's own governing.

He is a God of true judgment. The King 'will not judge by what His eyes see' because the One who sent Him does not. He sees the heart, as the choice of a shepherd boy to be king taught Israel, 1 Samuel 16:7, and He takes the side of the poor and lowly. The poor are not an afterthought in God's government; the verse mentions them first. He is also a God who strikes the wicked with the word of His mouth, and so His peace is not the peace of one who ignores evil but of one who deals with it.

He is the God of knowledge. The ground of the peace is that the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD 'as the sea is full of water.' Habakkuk 2:14 says it in nearly the same words, adding 'the glory.' The deepest need of the world, as the passage sees it, is not for stronger enforcement but for the knowledge of God, and the God of Isaiah is willing to be known. Violence is what happens when He is not known, and peace is what happens when He is.

He is also the God of the second time. In chapters 5 and 9 and 10 the refrain was that His hand was upraised and His anger not turned away. Here the same hand is stretched out 'a second time to recover the remnant of His people,' verse 11. The hand that struck is the hand that gathers. The God who disciplines is also the God who buys back, and He does it from places as far as Cush and the islands. He also gives the exodus a second life, drying the seas and rivers so that His people can pass.

There is a surprise in the way He treats the nations. The root stands as a banner for the peoples, and the nations seek Him. The enemies of verse 11, Assyria among them, are places from which His people are brought, and elsewhere Isaiah says that Assyria will be called 'My handiwork,' Isaiah 19:25. The God of Israel is the God of the nations, and His rescue extends to them.

For worship, the passage teaches us to praise a God who is not discouraged by the stump, who rules by knowledge rather than force, and who promises that the earth will one day be as full of Him as the sea is full of water.

crossReferences.note: God sends Samuel to Jesse of Bethlehem to find a king after Saul's rejection. Isaiah's choice of 'the stump of Jesse' sends the hearer back to this beginning: the dynasty is returned to its humble roots, and God starts again from there.

Job observes that there is hope for a tree: cut down, it sprouts again, and at the scent of water the stump will bud. Isaiah applies the same feature of nature to David's line, so that the stump of verse 1 is not a sign of death but of a root that still lives.

God tells Hezekiah that the surviving remnant of Judah 'will again take root below and bear fruit above,' and that the zeal of the LORD will accomplish it. It repeats the root-and-fruit image of Isaiah 11:1, and shows that the shoot imagery was also applied to Judah's survival in Isaiah's own day.

The Servant grows up 'like a tender shoot, and like a root out of dry ground,' with no stately form. It is the same picture of humble beginnings from the Servant's side, and shows that the glorious King of chapter 11 and the despised Servant of chapter 53 are one figure.

John the Baptist sees the Spirit descend and rest on Jesus, and the Spirit rests on the one who will baptize with the Holy Spirit. It is the clearest fulfilment of Isaiah 11:2 in the Gospels and uses the same idea of a Spirit that stays.

Jesus tells His critics to stop judging by outward appearances and judge justly. It echoes the King of Isaiah 11:3, who does not judge by sight or hearsay, and shows that He asks His followers to practise the justice He embodies.

The earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea. It is nearly identical to Isaiah 11:9 and shows that the same hope was known to two prophets from different centuries. Habakkuk adds the word glory, to show that to know God is to see Him.

In the new heavens and new earth the wolf and the lamb feed together and the lion eats straw, 'but the food of the serpent will be dust.' It repeats the peaceable kingdom and adds a line from Genesis 3:14 about the serpent, so that the cobra's den of Isaiah 11:8 is placed under the curse the serpent already received.

The bronze serpent on a pole, nes, gave life to anyone who looked. Isaiah 11:10 uses the same word for the banner. Jesus draws the line in John 3:14-15, and the lifted pole is a picture of how the nations will be drawn to the one who is lifted up.

The song of Moses says that the people the LORD 'bought' will pass by. Isaiah 11:11 uses the same verb of a second purchase and describes a second exodus. It sets the future gathering in the pattern of the first great rescue.

The two sticks of Joseph and Judah are made into one in God's hand, and the divided kingdom is united under one king. It is the picture of Isaiah 11:13, where Ephraim's envy and Judah's harassment cease, and it shows that the healing of the split was a hope widely shared.

A highway runs between Egypt and Assyria, and the LORD calls them 'My people' and 'My handiwork,' with Israel as a third in a blessing on the earth. It is the other side of the highway in Isaiah 11:16, and shows that the old enemies are not only conquered but brought into the family.

Paul quotes the Greek form of Isaiah 11:10 to show that the mission to the Gentiles was foretold. The Root of Jesse arises to rule the nations, and in Him they put their hope. It is the clearest New Testament quotation of the chapter.

The elder announces the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, who has triumphed, and John sees a slain Lamb with seven eyes, the seven Spirits of God. The title of Isaiah 11:10 and the Spirit of 11:2 meet in one scene, and the manner of the victory is shown to be the cross.

study.oneStory:
The shoot from Jesse answers a question that the story has been asking since Genesis 3: how will the line of the woman produce the one who defeats the serpent? In Genesis 3:15 the promise is of an offspring. In Genesis 49:10 the sceptre is given to Judah, in 2 Samuel 7 to the house of David, and by Isaiah's day the house looked finished. Isaiah 11 says that from a stump the promised offspring will come. It also uses Eden's own language: the child who plays beside the cobra's den, and the serpent whose food is dust, tell us that the old enmity is ended and that the One who ends it is the offspring of the woman.

The passage also joins the two great themes of the prophets: a king and a people. The first half is about the King and His Spirit, His justice and His peace. The second half is about the people, scattered in the world by the judgments of the earlier chapters, and the second exodus that brings them home. The hope that Israel might be restored and the hope that the nations might be blessed, which seem to pull in different directions, are joined in one banner. This was the promise to Abraham, that in him 'all the families of the earth will be blessed,' Genesis 12:3.

After Isaiah the story moves through exile and return, and the throne stays empty. The return under Cyrus gives a first gathering, but no king of David's line sits as the shoot. The long silence between the Testaments is a period of waiting on this chapter. Then Matthew begins with Jesse and David in the family tree, and a baby is laid in a manger in David's town. Jesus is baptized and the Spirit rests on Him, He judges with truth, and He is lifted up. Paul reads Isaiah 11:10 as the explanation for the church's mixed congregations of Jew and Gentile, Romans 15:8-12.

The story is still being completed. The King is raised and has sent His Spirit, and the nations are being gathered, but the wolf and the lamb are not yet at peace and the earth is not yet as full of the knowledge of the LORD as the sea is full of water. The church lives in the time of the banner, announcing the King to the nations.

The new creation is where Isaiah 11 is fulfilled. 'By its light the nations will walk,' and 'nothing unclean will ever enter it,' while the Root of David is called the bright Morning Star, Revelation 21:24 and 22:16. A multitude from every nation stands before the throne and before the Lamb, Revelation 7:9, and the 'holy mountain' of Isaiah 11:9 is the city where God dwells with humanity and where 'there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain,' Revelation 21:3-4. The shoot has become the tree whose leaves are for the healing of the nations, Revelation 22:2.

sermon.title: The Shoot from Jesse, the Nations, and Israel
sermon.why: Piper walks through all of Isaiah 11 in detail, tracing the shoot's character and reign, the peace of His global kingdom, the nations coming to Him, and the gathering of Israel's remnant, directly matching the four movements of this study and drawing out Christ's fulfillment of the prophecy.

quiz.q: What does the image of a shoot rising from 'the stump of Jesse' communicate?

options.text: New, Spirit-empowered life emerging from what appeared to be a finished, dead royal line.
options.note: This deliberately follows and contrasts with the felled forest of Assyria's pride in chapter 10, showing God's power in humble, unexpected growth.

options.text: That Jesse himself would be resurrected physically.
options.note: The shoot represents a coming descendant, not Jesse's own literal resurrection.

options.text: The permanent end of David's royal line with no future hope.
options.note: A shoot rising from a stump specifically signals continued, hopeful growth, not final ending.

options.text: A minor administrative appointment within David's existing court.
options.note: The imagery and the following description of Spirit-empowered, universal reign go far beyond a minor court appointment.

quiz.q: How does this coming King exercise justice, according to verses 3-4?

options.text: Not by mere outward appearance but with true righteousness, especially for the poor and lowly.
options.note: Verse 3 explicitly says He will not judge by what His eyes see or His ears hear alone.

options.text: By favoring the wealthy and powerful exclusively.
options.note: The text specifically highlights His righteous judgment for the poor and lowly, not the powerful.

options.text: By delegating all judgment to human courts.
options.note: The passage describes His own direct, personal exercise of judgment, not delegation.

options.text: By avoiding judgment altogether.
options.note: The text explicitly describes Him actively judging and deciding cases, not abstaining from judgment.

quiz.q: What does the peaceable kingdom imagery of verses 6-9, the wolf with the lamb, communicate?

options.text: A complete undoing of creation's violence, rooted in the earth being full of the knowledge of the LORD.
options.note: Verse 9 explicitly gives the reason: universal knowledge of the LORD produces this comprehensive peace.

options.text: A description of an ancient zoo exhibit.
options.note: This is symbolic, theological imagery about the effects of the Messiah's reign, not a literal zoological report.

options.text: A warning that predators will become more dangerous.
options.note: The imagery describes reconciliation and safety, the opposite of increased danger.

options.text: A purely political statement about international alliances.
options.note: The imagery is cosmic and creational in scope, rooted in universal knowledge of God, not merely political alliance.

quiz.q: How does Paul use Isaiah 11:10 in Romans 15:12?

options.text: He quotes it directly to show that the Root of Jesse's mission includes drawing the Gentiles, fulfilled in Christ.
options.note: This ties the passage's messianic hope directly to the New Testament church's mission to the nations.

options.text: He argues the verse applies only to ethnic Israel with no relevance to Gentiles.
options.note: Paul specifically applies the verse to Gentile inclusion in God's people.

options.text: He rejects the verse as inapplicable to the church age.
options.note: Paul affirms and applies the verse as fulfilled and relevant, not rejects it.

options.text: He uses it to argue against any Gentile mission.
options.note: Paul uses it to support, not oppose, the mission to the Gentiles.

quiz.q: What does the 'second exodus' language of verses 11-16 emphasize about the coming regathering?

options.text: God will gather His scattered people from every direction just as decisively as He once brought Israel out of Egypt.
options.note: The explicit comparison to the exodus from Egypt in verse 16 frames this as a comparably decisive act of divine deliverance.

options.text: It describes a minor, insignificant regional relocation.
options.note: The passage names numerous distant regions, Assyria, Egypt, Elam, Shinar, and the islands of the sea, indicating a comprehensive, significant gathering.

options.text: It predicts the exiles will never actually return.
options.note: The passage promises an actual, decisive gathering, not permanent exile.

options.text: It focuses exclusively on the northern kingdom, excluding Judah.
options.note: The text explicitly names both 'the exiles of Israel' and 'the scattered of Judah' together.

questions: This chapter's shoot rises from what looked like a completely dead stump. Where in your own life or circumstances do you need to trust that God can bring new life out of what feels finished or hopeless?

The coming King judges not by mere appearance but with true discernment for the poor and lowly. Where might you be tempted to judge people or situations only by surface impressions rather than seeking real understanding?

The peaceable kingdom flows from the earth being full of the knowledge of the LORD. How is growing in your own knowledge of God currently producing more peace, or less anxiety, in your relationships and circumstances?
The Root of Jesse becomes a banner drawing the nations to Himself. How are you actively participating in God's mission to draw people from every background to Christ?

God promised to gather His scattered people as decisively as He once delivered Israel from Egypt. What situation in your own life do you need to trust God to gather, restore, or redeem as thoroughly as that first great deliverance?

translationNotes.note: 'Branch,' netzer, is a different Hebrew word from the tsemach, Branch, of Isaiah 4:2, though both carry similar messianic freight; netzer may be reflected in Matthew's wordplay identifying Jesus as a Nazarene, Matthew 2:23.

'The rod of His mouth' and 'the breath of His lips' describe the power of His spoken word to execute judgment, imagery Paul draws on directly in 2 Thessalonians 2:8 describing the defeat of the lawless one at Christ's coming.

'A second time' explicitly frames this regathering as a second exodus, comparable to the first deliverance from Egypt, and the long list of regions named reflects the wide scattering of Israelites across the ancient Near East by this point in history.
